newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse says quality of trade improves.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse says quality of trade improves.

text.p: The appearance of shares and new financial instruments and better trading conditions characterised Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) activity in the first half of this year, a senior BSE official said on Monday.

"BSE turnover in the January-June period this year was at almost the same level as in the first half of 1996 but the structure of trade changed with new instruments appearing on the bourse," said the BSE director Pava Zecevic.
In January-June the volume of BSE trade stood at 1.2 billion dinars ($247.4 million) in 4,461 deals. In the whole of 1996, 7,942 deals were worth some 2.2 billion dinars.
Commercial paper accounted for some 51 percent of the six-month turnover, in trade which included deals in financial instruments and commodities.

A Yugoslav Securities Commission ruling last November that a portion of new issues of approved shares must be registered on the bourse resulted in the appearance this year of shares which were not traded in 1996. New stock issued by banks and companies wanting to increase their capital tends to be sold to known buyers but not to appear on the secondary market.
"The importance of them being registered is in securing the list of the issued shares and their owners," Zecevic said.
"It is not a classic form of listing...but what counts is that they are on offer. It is a tiny step towards an equity market."
Another novelty for the bourse was the sale for the first time of Yugoslav government 30- and 60-day treasury bills worth 100 million dinars, Zecevic said.
"Investors showed extremely high interest...and the entire first issue of T-bills was sold out," she said.
The government launched a second 200 million dinar issue last week. It carries a 3.5 percent monthly interest rate, down from 4.5 percent on the first issue.
For the first time, producers of various commodities appeared on the bourse issuing forward selling contracts with commodities as collateral.
"Although very few producers offered limited quantities of goods, it is of great significance as it is a new beginning, the first phase of a futures market," Zecevic said.
Conditions under which banks and firms borrow and repay their debt improved since the beginning of the year, with easier interest rates and longer maturity periods, she said.

"There are more and more deals with maturity longer than 15 days. Interest rates dropped to an average of 7.5 to 8.5 percent, although monthly rates are still high compared to their level in stable economies."
She said liquidity in the past months has improved. Low-risk state financial instruments remain popular.

Of the January-June turnover, bonds issued by the Serbian Commodity Reserve Agency from the portfolio of the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) accounted for 17 percent, NBY short-term bonds for 10 percent and government T-bills nine percent.
Zecevic said it was important that non-member brokerages were reporting their turnover and registering their transactions.
"Practically this means that the BSE data includes the majority of transactions on the domestic financial market and gives an overall, realistic picture of its development."
-- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254 ($ = 4.85 Yugoslav Dinars)
